newsitem.title: USA: Support for Dole remains below 40 percent in polls.
newsitem.headline: Support for Dole remains below 40 percent in polls.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
In a welter of opinion polls on the 1996 presidential race, one fact stands out: Support for Republican Bob Dole is stuck below the 40 percent mark.
Unless Dole can break through into the 40s, it does not take a political genius to predict that President Bill Clinton is heading for a comfortable victory in the Nov. 5 election.

Polls over the past month have shown Clinton's lead wavering between eight and 20 percentage points. But the swings are almost all due to fluctuations in support for the president. Support for Dole remains stable.
In a series of Reuters polls since early August, these were the support levels for Dole: 31 percent on Aug. 6, 36 percent on Aug. 22, 33 percent on Sept. 5, 34 percent on Oct. 1.
The Hotline political newsletter surveyed 50 national opinion polls taken in September. Dole exceeded the 40 percent mark in only three.
"It is true that Senator Dole needs to get above the 40 percent mark in the next week or so to make this a competitive race," said Linda DiVall, a Republican pollster advising the Dole campaign.
Dole will have a big opportunity on Sunday in the first of two presidential debates. But Clinton campaign officials are increasingly confident the president's lead is solid.
"The most striking thing about this race is that nothing has really changed since Memorial Day in May," Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said.
Dole recently started running more sharply negative television advertisements against Clinton, branding him a "tax-and-spend liberal."
There is little evidence the tactic is working. Clinton's approval ratings, though still high, have slipped a little -- but Dole's are also falling.
A Hotline poll this week found Clinton's popularity down three points in the past two weeks and Dole's down by the same amount.

In a series of interviews, voters said Dole's main problems were his age (73), his long record as a political insider, what is widely regarded as his lack of charisma and the Republican agenda of the past two years, which many people believe was too harsh.

"I usually have no qualms about voting Republican, but this year I'm a little hesitant. Dole is a little too old and too conservative for me," Jill McCray, a real estate agent from Midlothian, Virginia, said.
Joseph Kilcullent, an airport shuttle driver from Philadelphia, said he supported Republican George Bush in 1992 but would back Clinton this time.
"Things are going right, and I don't like Dole, maybe because of his age a little bit. The Republicans are messing with benefits for older people, and Clinton will protect them," he said.

In his television advertising this week, Dole is spending $800,000 on national network buys. The unusually large amount suggests he needs to project his message to the entire country. He is spending an additional $411,000 on national cable networks.
Dole stopped spending money this week in the Midwestern states of Iowa and Missouri but started spending in Oregon.
He has cut his time buying in California to $250,000 but is spending heavily in Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Connecticut and New Jersey -- all states where he trails Clinton.
